title: Design a Notification System for Events and Campaigns
prompt:
Design a notification platform that serves both real-time product events and scheduled or manually launched bulk campaigns. It must deliver email, SMS, mobile push, and partner/social-channel notifications while honoring user channel preferences and global do-not-disturb windows. Templates must support localization.

Assume tens of millions of messages per day and bursty upstream event traffic. Delivery must be at least once, but a user must not receive duplicate transactional notifications. Each channel needs independently configurable retry and backoff behavior.

Start with clarifying questions and a target SLO. Then cover:

- The API and durable state for event-triggered notifications, campaign creation, template versions, user preferences, and delivery status.
- Two explicit paths: an event-driven transactional path and a batch path that expands a cohort, applies rate control, and supports A/B sampling.
- The end-to-end path for a scheduled arrival reminder: schedule → event → queue → preference-aware router → channel worker → idempotent provider call → delivery callback.
- Idempotency boundaries, retry policies, provider failures, observability, and the difference between at-least-once delivery and an unachievable end-to-end exactly-once guarantee.

This is a writing exercise. Make assumptions explicit instead of silently designing for every possible notification product.

response.placeholder: State the workload and SLO assumptions first. Then draw the transactional and campaign paths, explain idempotency, and cover delivery failures and trade-offs.
response.reference_answer:
## 1. Scope and assumptions

I would first separate transactional notifications from campaigns. I assume transactional messages need low end-to-end latency and strong duplicate suppression, while campaigns optimize controlled throughput and auditability. The acknowledgement SLO is for a durable notification intent; delivery latency and provider acceptance are tracked separately by channel.

## 2. Durable contract and state

The API accepts an event or campaign request with an event ID or client idempotency key, recipient or audience definition, template version, locale inputs, and optional scheduled time. A durable notification-intent record stores the normalized payload, preference decision, chosen channel candidates, and a delivery key. Campaign definitions, immutable cohort snapshots, experiment assignments, template versions, and channel attempts are separate records.

A unique `(notification_kind, business_event_id, recipient_id, channel)` delivery key makes a retry return the same logical delivery instead of creating another one. The database write and queue publication use an outbox so a committed intent cannot be lost between services.

## 3. Two pipelines

For real-time events, producers write an event to a durable stream. A notification planner consumes it, resolves recipients and preferences, renders a localized template, creates idempotent delivery intents, and emits one work item per eligible channel.

For campaigns, a scheduler starts an immutable campaign run. A cohort service expands and snapshots the eligible audience, assigns A/B variants deterministically, and feeds a rate-controlled campaign queue. It uses separate rate limits per provider and channel so a large email campaign cannot starve transactional SMS. Both pipelines converge at the same preference, rendering, delivery, and status components.

## 4. Channel delivery and duplicate control

A router selects a user-approved channel outside the relevant do-not-disturb interval, with a documented fallback policy. Channel workers lease work, call providers with the delivery key when supported, and persist the provider response before acknowledging the queue message. A callback consumer maps provider webhooks back to the same attempt.

The queue is at least once: a worker can die after a provider call but before acknowledging it. End-to-end exactly once is not generally available because the provider is outside the transaction. The mitigation is an idempotency key at the provider, a durable attempt ledger, and conservative recovery for ambiguous calls.

## 5. Retries, controls, and operations

Each channel owns retryable-error classes, exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count, and a dead-letter review path. Preference changes and global quiet hours are rechecked immediately before a non-urgent send. I would monitor queue age, planner lag, campaign expansion rate, provider error rate, dedupe hits, attempts per delivery, callback latency, template failures, and per-channel acceptance and completion rates.

The central trade-off is isolation: enough shared infrastructure to keep one delivery model, but separate queues, rate budgets, and SLO dashboards so campaign load does not degrade transactional delivery.
